cues.text: ODYSSEY — BOOK XXI
The bow: pedigree, contest, recruitment, and the stringing.
And now the goddess put it in her mind — gray-eyed Athena,
in the mind of Icarius' daughter,\nwatchful-minded Penelope —
to set before the suitors the bow and the gray iron
in the halls of Odysseus: the contest,\nand the beginning of the slaughter.
She climbed the high stairway of her house\nand took the bent key in her strong hand —
a beautiful key of bronze, with an ivory handle —\nand went her way with her attendant women
to the last storeroom. There the master's treasures lay:
bronze, and gold, and iron wrought with labor.
And there lay the backsprung bow, and the quiver for\nthe arrows, with many groan-laden shafts inside —
gifts that a guest-friend gave\nhim when they met in Lacedaemon:
Iphitus, Eurytus' son, a man like the immortals.
The two had crossed paths in Messene,\nin the house of thoughtful Ortilochus. Odysseus
had come to collect a debt the whole people owed him:
for Messenian men had lifted sheep out of Ithaca —
three hundred, with their herdsmen —\nin their many-benched ships.
For their sake Odysseus came that long road on embassy,
a boy still, sent out by his father and the other elders.
And Iphitus came hunting horses — twelve mares he had lost,\nwith hard-working mules at suck beneath them —
the same mares that afterward became his death and doom,\nwhen he came to the strong-hearted son of Zeus,
the man Heracles, that expert in great deeds,\nwho killed him — a guest in his own house.
Ruthless: no shame before the gods'\nwatching eye, nor for the table
he himself had set the man; he killed him even so,\nand kept the strong-hoofed mares in his own halls.
Asking after these, Iphitus met\nOdysseus, and gave him the bow
that great Eurytus carried in the old days,\nand left to his son at his death in the high house.
And Odysseus gave him a sharp sword and a strong spear —
the start of a binding friendship; but they never knew
each other's tables: before that, the son of Zeus killed\nIphitus, Eurytus' son, that man like the immortals,
who gave the bow. And noble Odysseus never took\nit with him going to war in the black ships:
it stood in his halls at home, a memorial of a\nbeloved guest-friend; on his own land he carried it.
And when she reached that storeroom,\nthe shining among women,
and stepped up on the oak threshold — which a\ncarpenter once planed with skill and trued to the line,
and fixed the doorposts in it,\nand hung the shining doors —
at once she quickly loosed the thong from the hook,\nslid in the key, and shot back the bolts of the doors
with a straight thrust. And they bellowed like a bull\nat pasture in a meadow — so loud the beautiful doors
bellowed at the key's stroke;\nand they flew open before her.
She stepped up onto the high floor, where the chests\nstood full of clothing laid away in fragrance.
Reaching up from there she took the bow off its peg,\nbright in the bow-case that enclosed it.
With the case on her knees,
and wept aloud, and shrill, and drew out the master's bow.
And when she had taken her fill of tear-heavy mourning,\nshe went her way to the hall, to the lordly suitors,
holding in her hand the backsprung bow and the quiver\nfor the arrows, with many groan-laden shafts inside;
and beside her handmaids carried the box where the iron
lay in plenty, and the bronze:\nthe master's gear of contest.
And when she reached the suitors, shining among women,\nshe stood beside the pillar of the close-built roof,
holding her glistening veil before her cheeks,\na trusted handmaid standing on either side,
and spoke at once among the suitors, and said her word:
"Hear me, you lordly suitors,\nwho have fastened on this house
to eat and drink your way through it without ever a pause,
its master long gone; nor could you offer any\nother excuse in all this time, any word at all,
except your lust to marry me and take me to wife.
Well then, you suitors — come:\nhere stands your prize before you.
I set out the great bow of godlike Odysseus.
Whoever strings the bow most easily in his hands\nand shoots an arrow through all twelve axes —
him I will follow, forsaking this house, this house\nof my marriage, this beautiful house, full of all
that sustains life. I think I shall\nremember it even in my dreams."
So she spoke, and told Eumaeus, the noble swineherd,\nto set the bow before the suitors, and the gray iron.
In tears Eumaeus took them and laid them down;
and the cowherd wept on his side,\nwhen he saw the master's bow.
And Antinous rebuked them,\nand spoke a word, and named them:
"Idiot rustics! — brains that stop at the day's end!
Wretched pair, why are you\nstreaming tears, and stirring up
the heart in the woman's breast?\nHer heart lies deep enough
in grief already, since she lost her dear husband.
Sit and feast in silence — or take your bawling outside,\nthe two of you, and leave the bow right here,
a trial for the suitors none will\nslip through: for I do not think
this polished bow is going to be strung with ease.
There is no man in this whole company\nsuch as Odysseus was. I saw him myself —
I remember it well — though I was still a witless child."
So he spoke; but the heart in his breast was hoping\nthat he would string the bow and shoot through the iron.
In fact he was to be the first to taste an arrow
from the hands of blameless Odysseus —\nthe man he was dishonoring
that moment, sitting in his hall,\nand egging on all his companions.
And the sacred strength of Telemachus spoke among them:
"Ah — Zeus the son of Cronos has made me witless!
My own dear mother — sensible as she is — declares\nshe will follow another man and forsake this house;
and I laugh, and enjoy it, with my witless heart.
Come then, you suitors — since here stands your prize:
a woman whose like there is not now in all Achaea,\nnot in holy Pylos, not in Argos or Mycenae,
not on Ithaca itself, not on the dark mainland —
but you know that yourselves.\nWhy should I praise my mother?
Come — no dodges, no dragging it out; no more hanging\nback from the stringing of the bow. Let us see it!
And I myself might make a trial of the bow as well:
for if I string it, and shoot through the iron,\nthen it would be no grief to me that my honored mother
should leave this house and follow\nanother man — since I would stay behind
man enough at last to lift my father's beautiful prizes."
He spoke, and flung the crimson cloak from his shoulders,
rising to his full height, and put\noff the sharp sword from his shoulder.
First he set up the axes, digging one long\ntrench for all of them, trued to a line,
and stamped the earth firm round them.\nAmazement took every man
who watched — how squarely he set them,\nwho had never seen it before.
Then he went and stood on the\nthreshold and began to try the bow.
Three times he set it shaking, hot to draw it home;
three times he eased his force, hoping still in his\nheart to string the cord and shoot through the iron.
And now, hauling a fourth time,\nhis strength would have strung it —
but Odysseus shook his head,\nand checked him, keen as he was.
And the sacred strength of\nTelemachus spoke among them again:
"Ah — so I will be a weakling and a coward all my days!
Or I am too young yet, and cannot trust my hands\nto defend a man when someone picks a quarrel first.
Come then, you who are stronger than I am —\ncome try the bow, and let us finish out the contest."
So speaking he set the bow away from him on the ground,\nleaning it against the joined and polished panels,
with the swift arrow propped on the fine door-hook there,
and sat back down on the chair from which he had risen.
And Antinous spoke among them, Eupeithes' son:
"Up, all you companions — in order, left to right,\nstarting from where the wine is always poured."
So spoke Antinous, and his word pleased them well.
And the first to rise was Leodes, the son of Oenops,\nwho was their sacrifice-diviner, and always sat
in the farthest corner by the\nbeautiful mixing-bowl: to him alone
their reckless outrages were hateful;\nhe was indignant at all the suitors.
He now was first to take the bow and the swift arrow,
and went and stood on the\nthreshold and began to try the bow.
He could not string it:\nlong before that, hauling, his hands
gave out — his soft, unhardened hands;\nand he said among the suitors:
"Friends, I cannot bend it. Let another take it now.
Many chief men this bow is going to strip of\nlife and breath — since truly it is better far
to die than live on and miss the mark we gather\nhere for day upon day, forever, waiting on hope.
Now every man of you hopes, every heart is\nset on marrying Penelope, Odysseus' bedmate.
But once he has tried the bow, and seen — well,\nlet him woo some other fair-robed Achaean woman
with his bride-gifts then, and seek her; and let this one
marry the man who gives the most, and comes as her fate."
So he spoke his say, and set the bow away from him,\nleaning it against the joined and polished panels,
with the swift arrow propped on the fine door-hook there,
and sat back down on the chair from which he had risen.
And Antinous rebuked him, and spoke a word, and named him:
"Leodes — what a word has slipped the fence of your teeth!
A dreadful word, a bitter one —\nI am angry just to hear it —
that this bow, if you please, will strip our chief\nmen of life and breath — because you cannot string it!
No: your honored mother did not bear you the kind\nof man who has it in him to draw a bow and shoot;
but the other lordly suitors will string it, and soon."
So he spoke, and gave his orders\nto Melanthius the goatherd:
"Look alive, Melanthius — light a fire in the hall,\nand set a big bench by it with a fleece on top,
and bring out the great wheel\nof lard from the stores inside,
so we young men can warm the bow, and grease it with\nthe fat, and try it, and finish out the contest."
So he spoke; and Melanthius quickly\nkindled the unwearying fire,
and carried up the bench and set\nit there with a fleece on it,
and brought out the great wheel\nof lard from the stores inside.
With that the young men warmed the\nbow and made their trials — and still
they could not string it: they fell\nfar short of the strength it took.
But Antinous still held off, and godlike Eurymachus,
the suitors' chiefs: in prowess\nthey were far the best of them.
Now out of the house those two had gone together,\nthe cowherd and the swineherd of godlike Odysseus,
and after them Odysseus himself, the noble one, came out.
And when they were outside the doors and the courtyard,
he raised his voice and spoke to them with gentle words:
"Cowherd — and you, swineherd —\nshall I say a thing to you,
or keep it to myself? My heart tells me to say it.
What kind of men would you be, to fight for Odysseus,
if he came from somewhere — like that,\nout of nowhere — some god bringing him?
Would you fight for the suitors, or for Odysseus?
Speak out, as your heart and spirit bid you."
Then the cowherd answered him, the master of the oxen:
"Father Zeus, if only you would accomplish this desire:
that the man himself come back, and a god guide him home —
then you would learn my strength,\nand how my hands follow it!"
And in the same way Eumaeus prayed to all the gods
that Odysseus of the many designs\nmight come home to his own house.
And when he had proof of the true mind in both of them,\nhe found words again, and said to them in answer:
"He is home — here — I am the man myself.\nAfter suffering many pains,
I have come in the twentieth year to my fathers' land.
And I know that of all my slaves, to you two only my\ncoming is what you prayed for. Of the rest I have heard
not one man praying that I come home again.
So to you two I will tell the\nwhole truth of what shall be.
If a god brings the haughty suitors down beneath my hands,
I will find wives for you both, and give you possessions,\nand houses built near mine; and from that day
you shall be to me the companions\nand brothers of Telemachus.
And come — I will show you a plain sign besides,\nso you may know me for certain and trust it in your hearts:
the scar — the wound the boar dealt me with its white tusk
when I went to Parnassus with the sons of Autolycus."
So speaking, he drew the rags back from the great scar.
And when the two had seen it, and taken in each detail,
they wept, and threw their arms round thoughtful Odysseus,
and kissed his head and shoulders, welcoming him home;
and in the same way Odysseus kissed their heads and hands.
And the light of the sun would\nhave gone down on their weeping
had not Odysseus himself checked them, and said:
"Enough of weeping and wailing — someone coming out\nof the hall might see, and tell them there inside.
Go back in one at a time, not all together:
I first, you after. And let this be the signal:
all the others — all the lordly suitors —\nwill refuse to let the bow and quiver be given to me;
but you, noble Eumaeus, carry the bow up the\nhall and set it in my hands; and tell the women
to bar the close-fitted doors of their quarters,\nand if any one of them hears groaning or the crash of men
inside our walls, let her not run out,\nbut stay where she is, at her work, in silence.
And you, noble Philoetius:\nyour charge is the courtyard gates —
bolt them with the bar,\nand quickly lash the fastening on."
So speaking he entered the well-settled house and\nwent and sat on the stool from which he had risen;
and then the two slaves of godlike Odysseus came in too.
Eurymachus by now was handling the bow, warming\nit this side and that at the glow of the fire —
and even so he could not string it.\nHis proud heart groaned aloud,
and bursting out in anger he spoke a word and named it:
"Damn it — here is a grief for me,\nfor myself and for us all!
It is not the marriage I mourn\nso much, though that stings too:
there are plenty of other Achaean women, some right\nhere in sea-circled Ithaca, some in other towns.
No — it is that we fall so far short in strength\nof godlike Odysseus that we cannot string
his bow. A disgrace for even men unborn to hear of!"
Then Antinous answered him, Eupeithes' son:
"Eurymachus, it will not stand so —\nand you know it yourself.
Today, through all the land, is the feast of the god —\nhis holy day. Who could be bending bows? No —
set it down and be easy. And the axes: why not leave them
standing, all of them? No one,\nI think, will carry them off —
no thief is coming into the hall of Laertes' son Odysseus.
Come — let the cupbearer pour first-drops in the cups,
so we can make libation, and lay aside the curved bow;\nand in the morning tell Melanthius the goatherd
to drive in goats, the pick of all his herds,
so we can lay thigh-pieces on the\naltar of Apollo, lord of the bow,
and then try the bow, and finish out the contest."
So spoke Antinous, and his word pleased them well.
And heralds poured water over their hands,\nand young men crowned the mixing-bowls with drink
and served it round to all, with first-drops in the cups.
And when they had poured, and drunk\nas much as their hearts would have,
Odysseus of the many designs,\nwith craft in mind, spoke among them:
"Hear me, you suitors of the far-famed queen,\nwhile I say what the heart in my breast commands.
To Eurymachus above all, and to godlike Antinous,
I make my plea — since he spoke\nthis word too as it should be:
for now, let the bow rest; turn it over to the gods;
and in the morning the god will\ngive the mastery to whom he will.
But come — give me the polished bow, so among you I\ncan try my hands and my strength: whether the force
is still there, that once lived in my supple limbs,\nor wandering and neglect have destroyed it by now."
So he spoke; and they were all outraged past measure,\nin dread that he would string the polished bow.
And Antinous rebuked him, and spoke a word, and named him:
"You wretched stranger —\nnot a grain of sense in you, not a trace!
Is it not enough that you feast at your ease with us,
the great ones — never stinted of the meal, listening in
on all our speeches and our talk? No other stranger,\nno beggar, gets to listen to our speeches.
It is the wine that has you — the honey-sweet: it damages
any man who gulps it wide-mouthed past his measure.
Wine — it was wine that maddened the Centaur,\nfamous Eurytion, in the hall of great-hearted Peirithous,
on his visit to the Lapiths.\nAnd when the wine had maddened his wits,
raving mad he did his evil in Peirithous' house;
and grief seized the heroes,\nand they leapt up and dragged him
out through the porch to the open air, and shore away
his ears and nose with the\npitiless bronze; and he, his wits
destroyed, went off in his witless\nheart, hauling his ruin with him.
From that came the feud between Centaurs and men;\nbut he found the evil first for himself, heavy with wine.
Just so I proclaim great trouble for you,\nif you should string that bow. You will meet no kindness
in this land of ours — we will pack\nyou straight off in a black ship
to King Echetus, the maimer of all mankind,\nand out of his hands nothing will save you. Sit easy,
drink, and do not set yourself against younger men."
Then watchful-minded Penelope answered him:
"Antinous — it is not fine, and it is not just, to stint
the guests of Telemachus, whoever comes to this house.
Do you think — if this stranger strings the great bow\nof Odysseus, trusting his hands and his own strength —
that he will lead me home and make me his wife?
He himself has no such hope in his breast.
Let none of you sit at the feast here grieving
over that: it would not be seemly —\nno, and it is not thinkable."
Then Eurymachus, Polybus' son, answered her:
"Daughter of Icarius, watchful-minded Penelope,\nit is not that we think he will lead you off — unthinkable —
but we shrink from the talk of men and women:
that one of the baser Achaeans may say someday,\n'Men far weaker are wooing a blameless man's
wife — and they cannot even string his polished bow;\nand then some other man, a wandering beggar, came
and strung the bow with ease, and shot through the iron.'
So they will say; and for us that\nwould be shame heaped on shame."
Then watchful-minded Penelope answered him:
"Eurymachus — there is no fair fame in the land,\nand cannot be, for men who dishonor and devour the house
of their better. Why count this thing your shame?
The stranger here is very tall, and firmly built,\nand declares himself the son of a well-born father.
Come — give him the polished bow. Let us see it.
For I will say this outright, and it will be accomplished:
if he strings it — if Apollo grants him that glory —\nI will dress him in a cloak and a tunic, fine clothing,
and give him a sharp javelin, to keep off dogs and men,
and a two-edged sword; and I will\ngive him sandals for his feet,
and send him wherever his heart and spirit bid him go."
Then clear-headed Telemachus answered her:
"Mother mine — the bow: no Achaean has better right\nthan I to give it or to refuse it to whomever I will —
not one of all who lord it through rocky Ithaca,\nnor in the islands over toward horse-grazing Elis:
not one of them shall force me\nagainst my will, not even if I choose
to give the stranger this bow\noutright, to carry off for good.
Go into the house and see to your own work,\nthe loom and the distaff, and command your handmaids
to go about their work. The bow belongs to men —
to all men, and to me above all:\nmine is the power in this house."
In wonder, she went back into the house,\nfor she laid her son's clear-headed word to heart.
Climbing to her upper room with her serving-women,\nshe wept there for Odysseus, her dear husband, until
gray-eyed Athena cast sweet sleep upon her eyelids.
And the noble swineherd had taken up\nthe curved bow and was carrying it —
and the suitors, all of them,\nburst out shouting through the halls;
and a man of the arrogant young men would say:
"Where are you carrying that curved bow,\nyou pitiful swineherd —
you drifter? Soon enough,\nout with your pigs, alone, away from men,
the swift dogs you raised\nyourself will eat you — if Apollo
will only be gracious to us,\nand the other deathless gods."
So they spoke; and he set the bow down\nwhere he stood, carrying it no further,
frightened, because the crowd of\nthem was shouting through the halls.
But Telemachus, from the other side,\ncalled out his threat:
"Old father — carry the bow on.\nYou will soon be sorry, obeying them all.
Watch out, or younger though I am\nI will chase you into the fields
pelting you with stones. In strength I am the better man.
If only I stood as far above all the suitors in\nthis house — in force of hands and strength —
I would soon send more than one of them off in misery,\nout of our house: for they devise evils."
So he spoke; and all the suitors laughed at him sweetly,\nand let go their bitter anger against Telemachus.
And the swineherd carried the bow up the hall and\nstood by thoughtful Odysseus and set it in his hands.
Then he called out the nurse Eurycleia and said:
"Telemachus commands you, watchful-minded Eurycleia:
bar the close-fitted doors of the women's hall,\nand if any woman hears groaning or the crash of men
inside our walls, let her not run out,\nbut stay where she is, at her work, in silence."
So he spoke; and for her the word stayed wingless.
And she barred the doors of the well-settled halls.
In silence Philoetius slipped out of the house\nand barred the gates of the well-fenced courtyard.
Under the colonnade there lay a curved ship's cable
of byblus fiber; with it he lashed\nthe gates, and went back in,
and went and sat on the stool from which he had risen,
with his eyes on Odysseus.\nAnd he was handling the bow already,
turning it round and round, testing it this way and that,
for worms that might have eaten\nthe horn while its master was away.
And a man would say, with a glance at his neighbor:
"Quite the connoisseur of bows! An expert eye — a thief's!
No doubt he has bows like this one laid up at home —\nor means to make one. Look how he turns it over,
this way and that — the vagrant schooled in trouble!"
And another of the arrogant young men would say:
"May all his profit in life come out exactly as\nhis luck in ever managing to string that thing!"
So the suitors talked. But Odysseus of the many designs,
the moment he had hefted the\ngreat bow and eyed it everywhere —
as when a man skilled in the lyre and in singing\neasily stretches a string around a new peg,
making the twisted sheep-gut fast at either end —
so without haste, without effort,\nOdysseus strung the great bow.
Then his right hand took hold and tried the string,
and under his touch it sang sweet, like a swallow's voice.
A great ache took the suitors; the color changed in\nevery face; and Zeus thundered loud, showing his signs.
And much-enduring noble Odysseus was glad that the\nson of crooked-counseled Cronos sent him an omen;
and he took up the swift arrow that lay bare on the table
beside him — the rest were\nstored inside the hollow quiver,
the ones the Achaeans were shortly going to taste.
He set it on the bridge of the bow,\ndrew back the string and the notched butt
from the very stool where he sat, and let the arrow fly\nwith a straight aim, and did not miss a single axe —
from the first helve-ring clean on through: the arrow
heavy with bronze passed through and out.\nAnd he said to Telemachus:
"Telemachus — the guest who sits in your halls does not
disgrace you: I did not miss the mark, and I was not long
about stringing the bow. My strength stands yet unbroken —
not as the suitors' taunts would\nhave it, in their disrespect.
But now it is time that supper\ntoo be made for the Achaeans,
while there is light — and after that,\nthe other entertainments:
the dance and the lyre.\nFor these are the garnish of a feast."
He spoke, and signaled with his brows.\nAnd he slung on his sharp sword,
Telemachus, the dear son of godlike Odysseus,\nand closed his hand around his spear, and there beside him,
close by his chair, he stood —\narmed in the flashing bronze.
